T.topic_fa: راز اسم «بلک فرایدی»: پلیس فیلادلفیا این اسم را از سر کلافگی گذاشت، مغازه‌دارها خواستند عوضش کنند به «جمعه‌ی بزرگ» و شکست خوردند؛ سال‌ها بعد به‌جای عوض‌کردن اسم، معنایش را عوض کردند
T.topic_en: Black Friday was a cop's complaint. Shops tried to rename it 'Big Friday' and failed. Decades later they kept the name and rewrote what it meant
T.central_tension_fa: فکر می‌کنیم اسم برند را خودمان انتخاب می‌کنیم؛ ولی اسم را مردم می‌گذارند. مغازه‌دارها نتوانستند اسمی را که از آن متنفر بودند پاک کنند؛ فقط توانستند داستانش را عوض کنند، و همان اسم بدنام شد بزرگ‌ترین برند خرید دنیا.
T.central_tension_en: We think we choose our brand's name. The public does. The shops couldn't erase a name they hated; they could only rewrite its story, and the insult became the biggest shopping brand in the world.
T.working_hook_fa: اسم «بلک فرایدی» را فروشنده‌ها نگذاشتند. پلیس گذاشت، و منظورش تعریف نبود.
T.working_hook_en: Black Friday wasn't named by a marketer. It was named by the police, and they didn't mean it kindly.

cover_idea.object: chrome police whistle on a lanyard (monochrome), large, centred

key_sources.claim: Philadelphia police used the term in the 1950s for the chaos of suburban shoppers and tourists before the Army-Navy game; by 1961 merchants 'tried unsuccessfully to change it to Big Friday'; red-to-black is 'the officially sanctioned—but inaccurate—story', a late-1980s reinvention; not common nationwide as late as 1985

Philadelphia police, early 1960s: traffic jams, accidents, shoplifting; merchants tried 'Big Friday'; red-to-black profit idea 'untrue'; term grew nationwide only in the late 1980s when merchants spread that narrative

Researcher Bonnie Taylor-Blake: probably coined by a Philadelphia traffic cop; a 1961 PR newsletter reported merchants wanting 'Big Friday'; 'The effort failed'; red-to-black is 'an invented explanation'
Coined by Philadelphia police 'because they hated it'; a Strawbridge's executive later 'invented a new explanation' (profits into the black); retail historian Michael Lisicky

T.framing_note: Type 3 (secret behind a familiar name), pegged to Black Friday on 27 Nov. Spine: (1) this week every shop, app and inbox says 'Black Friday'; (2) the name came from Philadelphia police, more than 60 years ago: crowds, traffic, shoplifting, 12-hour shifts; 'black' = a bad day; (3) shopkeepers hated it and tried 'Big Friday' (by 1961). Nobody used it; (4) decades later, the turn: they stopped fighting the name and gave it a new story, 'the day the books go from red ink to black ink'. Historians call that story invented; it still won; (5) today the insult is a global retail brand; (6) lesson: you can't delete a name people already use; you can change what it means. Tell customers the story before they write it. Safe wording only: no single named coiner; coinage 'more than 60 years ago' (sources say 1950s / early 1960s / 1966); the profit story 'decades later' or 'in the 1980s'; never cite a first-print publication; never say Black Friday is the busiest day of the year (contested). Do not show real police insignia, real people, or any store's logo. Patagonia's 2011 ad may appear only as a one-line aside, without the 30% sales claim. One number on screen: 1961 (or 'Big Friday' as the visual punchline). Never name the UAE, Dubai or any emirate.
T.image_note: No owner upload needed: the story is about a name, not a product, and the sources' photos are news/stock images, not official brand material. Reels use generated objects and words-as-image (fx: words) only.
